articles.title: Bukele deploys thousands of soldiers to Haiti
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: El Salvador’s right-wing president, Nayib Bukele, announced on October 29, that he will deploy a military force of nearly 2,000 soldiers to Haiti. The Salvadoran president has justified the measure by citing the disappearance of four Salvadoran soldiers on October 18. The Salvadoran soldiers reportedly went missing following an armed attack in Croix-des-Bouquets, near the capital Port-au-Prince, involving the armored vehicle in which they were traveling. According to some reports , the attackers used very powerful weapons and explosives. Since then, the whereabouts of the soldiers remain unknown, and it is unclear whether they are still alive. According to Bukele, thousands of Salvadoran soldiers are conducting search operations. Several critics have claimed that the deployment amounts to a military invasion of Haiti. Bukele and unelected Haitian prime minister justify deployment The Salvadoran president has denied accusations of an invasion: “This is not an operation against the Haitian people, nor is it an invasion of Haiti. We are not a major power. We have no interest in coming to dominate the Haitian people, nor in laying our hands on Haiti’s wealth … All we want is for our four aviation technicians to return home.” In announcing the deployment, Bukele also addressed the issue of who is funding the operation: “We are practically the only ones paying for this operation. Although we receive a little logistical assistance from some other countries, it is with our own modest budget that we are covering 90% of the expenses.” Furthermore, Bukele justified , in a biblical tone, the presence of his soldiers by stating that El Salvador also knows the hardships of gang violence: “We have gone through the same suffering that Haiti is going through today. We have experienced a bloodbath that was even more terrible than what the Haitian people are suffering now … We are not coming to Haiti to make money, because no one is paying us for this. We’ve come to Haiti to fight the bad guys. But this is what I ask of you: Trust us, pray to the one true God, and ask Him to heal Haiti.” For his part, de facto Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé stated in a press release that the deployment of thousands of Salvadoran soldiers is not an invasion, but rather an operation of “bilateral and cooperative coordination” to locate the missing soldiers. Critics denounce deployment as further destabilization of Haiti Human rights advocates, on the other hand, have warned against foreign interventions that historically have further destabilized Haiti and increased violence. One of the countries in the region most closely aligned with the US, and a key part of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” bloc, El Salvador’s deployment is seen as far more than just a small regional nation’s military involvement. Donald Trump himself reportedly gave the Salvadoran president the green light for military action. Further, Bukele’s own comparison to gang violence in El Salvador draws attention to the various groups and communities that have denounced his iron-grip response in the country. Many say the pretext of gang violence was used to institute an ongoing state of emergency that stripped basic democratic rights and led to a systematic consolidation of power by Bukele’s loyalists. Investigative journalists at El Faro also exposed that Bukele made a secret pact with the gangs before implementing his iron-grip model. The suggestion that a similar approach needs to be taken in Haiti is exactly what human rights activists have been sounding the alarm about. But understanding the implications of El Salvador’s deployment requires looking beyond the immediate search for the missing soldiers. Haiti’s security crisis is inseparable from the political instability, foreign interference, and historical structures of domination that have shaped the country for generations. Political destabilization or gang problem? The four Salvadoran soldiers in Haiti were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a UN-authorized military deployment of personnel from different countries allegedly to help control the security situation in the country. The GSF has come under heavy criticism as the latest iteration of the UN occupation of Haiti which has already caused immense harm to the Haitian people and has been incapable of “controlling” the situation of violence. In Haiti, public trust in the transitional leadership is already low. High-ranking officials, including former National Police Chief Frantz Elbé, faced widespread public backlash and demands for removal following allegations of political corruption, failure to protect citizens, and covert ties between elements of his police force and local gangs. Citing this corruption, experts say the situation in Haiti is much deeper than a gang crisis. “These gangs regularly receive weapons and ammunition from the United States,” says Venezuelan academic Guillermo Barreto. “This action indicates a project that seeks to make the functioning of a nation unviable. But this attack on the Haitian nation is not recent. Haiti has been under siege by imperial powers since its independence. “

articles.title: Half a million join youth-led protests in France
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Saturday, October 31, opened as another day of mass mobilizations across France. For almost two months – led by high school and university student demands for stronger public education – hundreds of thousands of people have been joining demonstrations against the policies of President Emmanuel Macron and successive administrations. According to student unions , at least 500,000 people joined the demonstrations on Saturday, including 200,000 in the capital. “We are now in the sixth week of mobilization by high school students and, more broadly, the youth,” Christophe Benoît, deputy general secretary of the General Confederation of Labor (Confédération Générale du Travail, CGT) in Lille, told BreakThrough News . “It’s a movement best summed up in the words of a high school student speaking at a recent assembly: ‘We see the social hardship of our parents and we see our own future reflected in it.'” Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education Students and youth have tabled demands to strengthen the public education system in France. These include investment in school infrastructure, ending the course selection platform Parcoursup, and ensuring fair and equitable access to higher education. Their demands are clearly linked to grievances raised by other groups during Macron’s presidency, which have warned against the devastating impact of raising the retirement age , eroding workplace rights, and leaving the cost-of-living crisis unchecked. “Against the politics of Macron” Speaking from the demonstration in Paris on Saturday, Maurizio Coppola from the International Peoples’ Assembly (IPA) emphasized the protests are taking place “against the austerity measures, against the politics of Macron.” Over the past ten years, Coppola added, these policies have been “dismantling salaries and social services.” Student protests have maintained a decisively anti-fascist character. Source: Jean-Luc Mélenchon/Facebook The convergence of the youth and student movement with trade unions and groups like the gilets jaunes , the Yellow Vests, has deeply shaken Macron’s and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s position. Faced with a general mobilization based on clearly progressive demands, authorities responded with violence , with dozens of injuries and thousands of student arrests reported since the protests began. An authoritarian turn in France? The state’s response has been so openly violent as to raise serious concern among human rights organizations. Amnesty International France contextualized parts of this response as part of a possible authoritarian turn by the country’s authorities. “A state that adopts authoritarian practices seeks to silence dissenting voices by restricting space for expression,” they wrote. “In France today, the right to demonstrate is under serious attack, with a series of protest bans, arrests and police repression.” The government has also attempted to discourage participation in the mobilizations by promoting and imposing protest bans and restrictions. Among other things, the route of Paris’ Saturday march was contested in court until the very last minute. High school and university students have been demanding more investment into public education. Source: Union étudiante/Facebook While labor and student unions pushed for a march in central Paris, the city’s police administration insisted on moving it to a more distant zone. Organizers contested this imposition in court, warning that the decision not only threatened to create chaos but also represented a notable attack on the right to protest. Even though the courts ruled in favor of the organizers, the Council of State – a body that acts as the highest administrative court and advisor to the government – overruled this decision and forced last-minute changes. Protesters in Paris joined the demonstration anyway, just as thousands of people took to the streets in other cities. General strike on November 5 The success of the movement continues to encourage new mobilizations, including, notably, a general strike on November 5. “It’s a general strike against Macron, against his system, against the war economy he has implemented,” Coppola said. “This solidarity cannot be stopped by some small measures, this solidarity cannot be stopped by the repression the French state is applying to the movement.” “We are dealing with questions of what kind of society we want,” Benoît emphasized, referring to the general strike. “It’s absolutely essential that the labor movement join forces with the youth to win real progress – for the entire population, too – against the capitalist policies we’ve been suffering from in France for decades now.” “We need a movement, a general movement, and we need to hit those who are really making the decisions in this country, that is to say, the employers.” By last Thursday, the CGT alone had already noted 185 industrial action announcements ahead of November 5. Student unions announced additional actions in the coming week – including a call to occupy high schools and universities – to support the general strike and protest demands.

articles.title: Gulf states scramble to avert another U.S.-Israeli war on Iran they cannot stop
articles.author: Mitchell Plitnick
articles.content: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye sent top security officials to Tehran as fears grow of a renewed U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran. With little leverage over Trump, the Gulf states face devastating consequences if the war resumes.

articles.title: Political Capitalism in Perspective: An Interview with Dylan Riley
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: In this interview with Historical Materialism , Dylan Riley offers an anatomy of his concept of ‘political capitalism’ in dialogue with theorists of technofeudalism and those who claim we are returning to a ‘normal capitalism’. He reflects on how the Left should think about the role of material interests in the struggle against a rising Far Right under political-capitalist conditions, and assesses Trump II in light of recent events . Teddy Paikin : In your recent piece in the Ideas Letter and in several contributions to the New Left Review , you and Robert Brenner have further developed the ‘political capitalism’ thesis, the view that capitalist reproduction increasingly relies on upward redistribution via ‘politically engineered support for high asset prices’ rather than traditional forms of investment and accumulation. You describe this process as a mutation of capitalism under specific circumstances, especially during periods of stagnation. Could you speak about the inspirations behind and development of this idea alongside Robert Brenner? Dylan Riley : If you look at the line of heterodox Keynesianism coming out of Alvin Hansen, there is a hinting toward an idea that secular stagnation goes hand in hand with the increasing importance of rent-seeking. That’s very explicit in his work on the Great Depression. You could say that some of this stuff was taken up by Baran and Sweezy in the monopoly-capitalism thesis. Although I’m not really an exponent of the monopoly-capitalism thesis – I don’t think that describes the current dynamics of capitalism – I do think it is useful in examining the changing role of political power in determining the rate of return. And, as I’ve made clear in a number of writings, I think that Max Weber is essential here to understanding what’s going on. Weber coined the term ‘political capitalism’ to refer to economic activity that is profit-oriented but relies predominantly on political means. TP : In your piece for the Ideas Letter , you reject two alternative explanations of the contemporary transformations in capitalism. One is the idea that today’s capitalism is nothing but a return to a ‘normal capitalism’ with profit rates comparable to those at the turn of the century. The other is the technofeudalism thesis which, as you’ve mentioned elsewhere, is a renewed monopoly-capitalism thesis. Could you clarify your refutation of these two views and specify how you think the political-capitalism framework better explains mutations in contemporary capitalism? DR : With respect to the ‘return to normal capitalism’ thesis, we could say that, since the publication of Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century , there is a notion that capitalism has been a very high-inequality, low-growth regime, except for this exceptional period, roughly from 1945 to 1973, in which it was a high-growth, relatively low-inequality regime. In support of this idea, some scholars make use of the Angus Maddison data on GDP growth to show how slow growth was in the nineteenth century, sometimes going all the way back to the Roman Empire. There is a conceptual and an empirical point I’d like to make about the use of these long-run GDP statistics over time. The conceptual point is that, if it’s true that capitalism is, for the most part, a low-growth regime, you would have to reject most of what Marxists have thought of as distinctive to capitalism since the fifteenth century, which is that this is a system that uniquely in world history was able to engender rapid economic growth and development. To deny that seems perverse to me. Among other things, it would be impossible to explain the British breakout from the Malthusian cycle, or the emergence of the First or Second industrial revolutions, and massive increases in productivity over time. So, the question that remains is, what’s going on with these long-run data series that seem to show relatively low growth? I think that’s a very important question. My sense – and it is only a sense, because I really need to do some work on this – is that these very broad indicators, especially when you include different places across the globe, essentially blend together economies where you already had a breakthrough to modern capitalism with places where you clearly did not. Does it make any sense to even talk about national growth rates in a country like pre-unification Italy, where you’re putting the Po Valley together with the large landed estates of the South? This could also apply to the United States, if you’re thinking about aggregate growth statistics that combine the South and the North. Now, turning to the technofeudalism thesis, first articulated by Cédric Durand and then cashed out in a somewhat different form by Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean, among others, the basic idea is that in the current period you have platforms whose value expands simply by increasing the number of their users. You can think about it in comparison to the automobile, for example. If one person purchases a car, the utility of that car is individual to that person. It is either useful or it is not useful. It doesn’t matter if other people have the same car or have a different car; the utility of that individual car is still the same. But, with platforms – social media platforms being perhaps a key example of this – the value of the platform increases as the number of users that use that platform increases. And the idea of technofeudalism, as I understand it, is that this process allows for the creation of a rent that can be appropriated by the owners of platforms, regardless of how much they have (or have not) invested in improving the technical capacity of their programmes. The obvious upshot of this is that you have many platforms that can rake in a lot of profit even though they may be technically inferior to alternative platforms. Ultimately, the profits that they collect are a form of monopoly or monopsony rent. I think this describes something important about what is going on, but my general sense is that there still is a considerable amount of competition among the big tech companies, such that, as a global description of the economy, I’m dubious of the technofeudalism thesis. However, I would say that, from my perspective, one of the virtues of the technofeudal literature is that it does try to periodise capitalist development and recognise that there’s something truly new going on, and I think that’s an intellectual virtue. TP : In your view, does political capitalism offer a more robust framework than ‘neoliberalism’ for understanding capitalism since the 1980s? Or are these two separate and complementary processes? DR : That’s a great question. My general view is that neoliberalism is the ideological form of political capitalism. It’s the ideology of political capitalism, and, like a lot of ideologies, it is a deeply misleading guide to the actual process of what’s going on. The rise of neoliberalism corresponds almost perfectly to the slowdown in growth in the 1970s. But the reality of neoliberalism – although it’s shrouded in the praise of markets and market allocation – is primarily political. It is an ideology of markets combined paradoxically with an ever more aggressive use of political power to shape profitability. But neoliberalism as an account of the actual dynamics of capitalism offers a terrible guide. It’s the ideological envelope in which political capitalism unfolded. TP : That’s very counterintuitive, because one wouldn’t expect an ideology which is based on market fundamentalism and a harsh separation of the political and the economic to develop a regime of accumulation in which the capitalist class becomes so dependent upon the state for its reproduction. DR : Let’s just remember what Marx says in The German Ideology : reality appears upside down as in a camera obscura . The point about ideology is not that it reflects reality; the point is that it inverts it. What is the ideology of capitalism in its classic phase? Well, to put it very simply, it is to describe a system of social production that is characterised by a very intricate global division of labour, in which all of the parts are linked to all the other parts, as if it were the very opposite – that is to say, a society of petty commodity producers. This is not the first time in the history of capitalism that the ideological envelope would point in the opposite direction of the social reality. TP : Your writings on politics under political capitalism emerged from a comparison with the theorisation developed by Przeworski and others of the nature of postwar capitalism. This was a period of sustained economic dynamism creating the conditions for the survival of capitalist democracy through a positive-sum form of capital accumulation in which wages and profits rose simultaneously, thereby undergirding a class compromise. But, with the advent of secular stagnation in the 1970s, this compromise disappeared as capitalists became less interested in making productivity-enhancing investments and moved toward rentier strategies of reproduction. From what I understood of the stagnation thesis, the basic political implication of your argument is an inability of traditional Keynesian methods and a repetition of the postwar welfare state to resolve capitalism’s current predicament. How do you think we should adapt our politics to political-capitalist conditions? Can you compare your view with what you believe follows politically from the technofeudal and ‘normal capitalism’ theses? DR : Maybe the comparison would be the best way forward. If we take Piketty and his many followers’ line of argument, the idea is that, at some point in the 1970s, things went off the rails and we got increasing inequality. It’s a little mysterious exactly why that happened. I find the r > g presentation to be descriptive, not explanatory. But the idea, politically, is that what must happen is a reconstruction of the classic social-democratic model of politics. For Piketty, the problem has been the rise of a kind of Brahmin Left, along with a series of political mistakes by centre-left parties. I think this view is widely shared on a certain sector of the Left – that we should try to correct centre-left parties that have somehow forgotten they were supposed to appeal to the working class. Somehow, we are supposed to remind their leaderships to be better social democrats. It strikes me that the problem with that position is that it ascribes what has been a very widespread collapse in the social-democratic project to contingent political mistakes. But how could it be that the Democratic Party, the Labour Party, the French Socialists, whatever remains of the Italian Communist Party, and the SPD all made the same mistake at the same time? How could that be just a contingent political error? The idea of a rerun of classic mid-century social democracy doesn’t seem to me to be a particularly workable idea for different reasons. One is that, as I have said, it really misunderstands that the contemporary working class itself is very fragmented. We need to somehow address those fragmentations, not pretend that an economic message is going to lead automatically to political unity. I don’t think that’s the right way forward. The other thing is I find that the rebooted social-democratic arguments tend to be very nation-state-oriented in their outlook. The people who argue for this kind of politics are willing to make a lot of concessions to xenophobia, which I find to be antithetical to a genuine left project. I think we need to think about a project that is both sensitive to the different articulations within the working class and is consistently internationalist. Those are both necessities for me. On the technofeudalism front, the politics of technofeudalism relies on the idea that there’s a real basis for a cross-class compromise between those segments of capital that are being exploited by the technofeudalists and the working class, and I’m a little sceptical of that argument as well. Politically, the upshot is not that different from the idea of rebooting social democracy – even though the analysis on which it is based is very different. TP : It seems to want to reboot the idea of a failed bourgeois revolution. DR : That’s a good way of putting it. You could say that in some ways it reflects historical reality because we’ve now fallen behind the French Revolution ( laughs ). But thinking beyond capitalism is more where I would like to end up. TP : Given that capitalists today depend increasingly on the state for their income, do you think that it follows from the political-capitalism thesis that capturing the state and using it to impede this kind of upward redistribution should be a central aspect of socialist politics and strategy? What kind of new relationship to the state do you think political capitalism implies? DR : I think there’s an enormous opening for the Left in what’s going on, because you could say that the political power of capitalism has always been the relative separation of the economic from the political, thereby allowing the economy to be treated as a realm of technocratic and non-political decision-making. Obviously, that is being completely overturned at this point. You see it even in the US, in just the regular conversations among the mainstream press that Trump is a communist because he’s handing out money to his friends. So, I think we have an opportunity here. We need to be thinking about the use of political power in new ways that have to do with breaking our dependence and reliance on enormous and unaccountable private actors for determining the growth path of all of our societies. I also think we need to think about technological development as a political choice as well. TP : One might have expected the zero-sum dynamics of political capitalism to have reignited class struggle, but, given the decline of the organised labour movement since the neoliberal period, what we’ve seen instead are renewed forms of populism on the Left and Right – or sometimes ‘neo-Bonapartisms’, as you put it – and the rise of nativism. So how can you explain the failure of an organised socialist Left and labour movement to re-emerge within the present context? And how do you think that is connected to the rise of nativism among workers? DR : I think the turn to the right among a segment of the working class is the most difficult problem that the Left faces today. You see this in the recent elections and the AfD. But the idea that class struggle would heat up as capitalism became less dynamic, or less able to deliver material goods, has turned out not to be true at all. As you can see by the whole history of West-European social democracy, the power of workers has been greater in those periods when there have been gains to share, at least within the context of established electoral systems. The reason for that is obvious: it’s really under those conditions that working-class parties can deliver material gains for their constituents. So, there was a virtuous and self-reinforcing cycle during the boom years after the Second World War, by which workers’ parties won gains that then increased their legitimacy at the polls, which allowed them to win further gains. All of that, however, was dependent on the long economic boom of the postwar period. The problem is that as that boom receded, it was not the case that workers were going to jettison reformism and go over to revolution. The reason that’s not the case is because there are lots of other strategies available to specific segments of the working class that allow them to defend their material interests, but that are not class strategies. There’s organising along lines of nationalist exclusivity: xenophobia is one form; in some countries, racial identity is an avenue, or in some cases various forms of credentialling. There are many ways in which this can happen, some of which are more reactionary and anti-democratic than others. But there’s a wide suite of available strategies that are open to workers in moments of slower growth or economic downturn. And it’s very difficult to get to a class strategy in the context of economic slowdown. This was most fully laid out by Przeworski in Capitalism and Social Democracy . I think it’s important for the Left to think about the material reasons that workers turn to the right, over and above – or entwined with – whatever ideological reasons might also exist. TP : This point is connected to your argument in a recent piece in Sidecar on the question of material interests in which you argue – against what you call a ‘simplified rational choice or “analytical” Marxism’ – that it is insufficient simply to invoke working-class material interests. In fact, it could be counterproductive when no concrete horizon of socialist politics exists. DR : The politics of the contemporary period needs to be a politics that makes tangible, in whatever ways possible, forms of life that are non-capitalist and collective, that make the possibility of an alternative real to people so that they can orient their interests in that direction. This may sound like a purely social-theoretical question, but it’s absolutely crucial. We need to think about futures as real in a way that sometimes some on the Left have been reluctant to do. If you think about the way people live their lives: you live your life toward what’s coming. You need to have an image of what that might be, and that is a decisively important political matter. What we really shouldn’t be doing is saying we need to reconstruct the mid-century class compromise. That is a way of envisioning the future that is utterly nostalgic, and it seems to me we don’t want to be in that position. TP : In creating that kind of horizon, what role do you think Marxist concepts have to play in the renewal of class struggle? Perry Anderson ended a recent article in the New Left Review with the line: ‘Ideas incapable of shocking the world are incapable of shaking it’. Why do you think that Marxist and socialist vocabulary no longer has the same power it had in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in creating that concrete alternative? How could it be adapted to participate in a contemporary making-concrete? DR : I wish I had a concrete answer. I only have a methodological answer. I think what Perry was saying – and this derives from Gramsci and others in the Marxist tradition – is that we need to think about politics as the articulation of a concrete fantasy. It is something which is tangible and almost aesthetic in a way and that people can think about and orient themselves toward. One of the ideas that has to be abandoned is that to be a materialist, or to be a historical materialist in particular, means that one doesn’t take ideas seriously. That’s completely untrue. It’s never been true. If it were true, why did Marx spend most of his energy and his greatest book essentially unfolding a critique of ideology? The readers of Historical Materialism know this, but I guess it is just worth emphasising: the problem is that if we don’t do that work, it’s not that the future or imaginaries cease to exist; it’s that they’re simply occupied by the Right. When we take a big step back and think about the position of the Left in the current period, there are many things that are very encouraging, especially compared to where it was in the 1990s. But we certainly do not have a vision of the future which is as total or as vivid as what the Silicon Valley tech guys are promoting with artificial intelligence, among other things. But the Marxist tradition is completely irreplaceable. Even its basic model of what it means to be a human being is about as good as anything out there, especially for these questions about orientation to the future. I just think it’s completely irreplaceable, and we have to continue to work to develop it and to update it for the circumstances that we’re currently facing. TP : It hasn’t lost any of its analytical power, but it does seem to have lost a degree of political force when considered in historical perspective. DR : This is not the first time, I suppose, in the history of Marxism or the history of the working-class movement, that there’s been this gap between analytical power and political relevance. But I think that the current moment, as dark as it is, does create opportunities because it’s so revelatory of what could be done, for example, with the modern state, were it to be reconfigured in ways that might make for a better future. TP : I’d like to get your current assessment of Trump II, and how you relate it to your thesis on political capitalism. Is Trump a kind of expression of political capitalism or a shift to something else? How does the change from Trump I to Trump II modify your view of the political nature of Trumpism? DR : I definitely interpret Trump as the apotheosis of political capitalism. It’s the whole thing taken to this unbelievable extreme. It’s almost too easy; I’m almost reluctant to say this, but how do you theorise this? The thing about Trump II is that you can’t theorise it just as a political phenomenon because it’s also a giant system of plunder. It’s quite different in that respect from Trump I. Many of his actions are essentially undertaken just to squeeze, extort, and extract. In terms of the relation between Trump I and Trump II, historians will have to approach this. Presumably, someone will write a three-part analysis of the age of Trump in which the Biden years are going to play a crucial role. Trump I was this quite shambolic, incoherent affair. He didn’t even think he was going to win. He came in; he didn’t really have a cadre, and they didn’t really have a programme for governing. With Trump II, they came into office with a very well-articulated strategy, with Russell Vought and Stephen Miller as the primary driving forces and ideologues behind this, and they’ve carried it through to some effect. The problem of Trumpism is Trump. He constantly gets in the way of what they should be doing, and so it never can quite gel as a coherent thing because he does crazy and erratic stuff. I’m sure, for example, that there are theories about how Trump’s war with Iran somehow reflects the geopolitical interests of the US, but I’m sceptical about this. I think a lot of this behaviour is just erratic and irrational, alongside the self-enrichment of his own personal familial group. I think this behaviour gets in the way of the project that they would like to be pursuing, which is much more well-articulated by a figure like J.D. Vance or even Stephen Miller than it is by Trump and his super-immediate entourage itself. He’s a peculiar figure because you could say his very particular attraction is bound up with his weaknesses. The only person with that kind of politics who could actually win an American election is Trump as a personality. But, precisely because of what he is as a personality, the project also can’t entirely be carried through, because he’s so utterly venal in everything. We’ll see what happens at the election. The unpopularity of this project is just astonishing; it’s basically just very hardcore supporters who are still with him at this point. Unless something dramatic happens, it looks like they’re in for a beating in the immediate term at the midterm elections. The problem is, though, none of the big structural problems of American politics are going to be resolved in any way, and structural problem number one is what to do with the working class. Dylan Riley is Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley and the author or co-author of six books. He studies capitalism, socialism, democracy, authoritarianism, and knowledge regimes in broad comparative and historical perspective. His most recent work focuses on the relationship between democracy and capitalism, particularly in its current phase. He is also at work on two larger book projects: a collection of essays provisionally entitled Science, Ideology, and Method , and a comparative historical analysis of democratisation in Germany, Italy, Japan, France, the UK and the US from c1200 to c1950 provisionally entitled Special Paths . articles.title: Final vote count for Israeli elections yields no clear winner
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Israel’s Central Elections Committee (CEC) released the final vote count on Friday, October 30, confirming that neither major political coalition managed to reach the 61-seat majority threshold necessary to form a government in the 120-seat parliament (known as Knesset). The results show that the pro-Netanyahu bloc secured 53 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot reached 48 seats. Meanwhile, Arab-led lists combined attained 19 seats, achieving an all-time high record in the history of Israel’s Knesset. The complete official results will be formally presented to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, November 4 once the CEC finalizes the review of any pending complaints or errors. Read more: Israel’s elections: all roads lead to genocide What do these results mean and what comes next? The outcome indicates a political deadlock that may be resolved with one of the following four options: Eisenkot’s bloc allying with Arabs The formation of an alliance that combines the 48-Eisenkot’s bloc with the 19 seats of both Arab-led lists to reach a 67-seat majority. However, it seems that there is no consensus between the parties within Eisenkot’s bloc on the possibility of a partnership with Arab factions. Broad unity government combining Nenyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s bloc Some analysts speculate that the Likud party led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could try to build a broad national coalition by teaming up with Eisenkot’s bloc. Nonetheless, clashing electoral campaign agendas on each side would obstruct this option. As ousting Netanyahu was one of the main goals of Eisenkot’s coalition, either this bloc breaks its campaign promise, or Netanyahu steps down, abandoning his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies. Netanyahu’s bloc pulling individual right-wing defectors from Eisenkot’s bloc To hit the 61-seat threshold required to form the government, Netanyahu may need to convince individual lawmakers or an entire party from Eisenkot’s bloc to defect and join his coalition. At least 8 defectors are needed to accomplish that. Although right-wing opposition figures like Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman share common ground with Netanyahu on issues related to Israel’s security, their political rivalry with him makes this scenario less probable. No agreement leading to new elections If neither coalition manages to form a government, the Knesset will automatically dissolve, with new elections to be held in the spring of 2027. During these months of stalemate, Netanyahu continues to hold office as caretaker prime minister. Election results trigger protests in Israel The outcomes of the elections pushed crowds to take to the streets across Israel, calling on Eisenkot to break the deadlock by forming an unprecedented coalition with Arab-led parties. Protesters also gathered near Netanyahu’s house, demanding an end to Israel’s genocidal aggression on Gaza, and accusing his government of using state security forces to keep him in power. It is worth noting that an investigation has been initiated by the Israel Security Agency ( Shin Be t) and the Institute for Intelligence and Special Operations ( Mossad ) into allegations of illegal campaign funding from Qatar and Türkiye to boost Arab voter turnout.

articles.title: ‘The Klan never stopped’: Two Black families fight for justice in Mississippi
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Marquell Bridges says the story the public’s been sold about what happened right before Senatobia Sgt. Hunter Foster shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley was a lie from the start. The Mississippi-based organizer and founder of the Building Bridges Coalition tells Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek police at Walmart were never responding to a shoplifting call, that no one in the car has been charged, and that Baby Kohen’s death is part of a long pattern of impunity for racist murder in Mississippi, from Emmett Till to the unsolved 2022 death of Rasheem Carter. Bridges breaks down Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s ruling Foster was “justified” in opening fire, weeks after a Jackson County grand jury declined to bring charges in 18-year-old Nolan Wells’s death, saying it was “consistent with drowning.” As calls for justice for Nolan Wells and Kohen Wiley spread from HBCUs and campuses in the South to cities across the US, Bridges says families cannot expect justice from a system he argues still carries the deep racist roots of the Klan: “Our governor, Tate Reeves, was seen in a picture with Confederate flags, at Nazi parties and in blackface,” Bridges says. “These people are the Klan …. The rest of the world moved forward, but nothing ever changed in Mississippi.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! ****** Rough transcript follows: There’s two Black families in Mississippi dealing with horror, tragedy, and complete injustice, and two official verdicts that have come down to basically the same thing. Mississippi authorities are saying there’s nothing to see here, move on, don’t look too closely at these issues. The first case involves 1-year-old Coen Whaley, who was sitting in his mother’s lap in a car in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia when a white police officer, Hunter Foster, opened fire on the car. Foster was responding to a call that Whaley’s mother and her friend had stolen diapers. He shot at her car as she pulled out of a parking space. A bullet went through Coen’s side and killed him. Last week, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office ruled the shooting justified, despite Coen’s mother and several witnesses saying they were never interviewed. The state has not released body cam footage or the overhead video from the parking lot. Days before the shooting, Hunter Foster was accused of making a racially offensive remark to a co-worker, and two earlier misconduct accusations against him have since come out. The Senatobia police chief, who took no action against him, was fired in September after it was revealed he routinely used racist slurs in private texts. Then there’s Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old Black college student who went on a 4th of July boat trip to Horn Island off the Gulf Coast. His body was found in the water days later. A grand jury declined to bring charges, saying the evidence was consistent with drowning, yet acknowledged bruising on the back of his head and said the cause of that injury remains uncertain. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family listed his manner of death as undetermined, and his family is demanding a federal investigation. In both cases, the state has closed the book, but people are refusing to allow that. Students from high schools and HBCUs are taking to the streets. Joining us now is Marquelle Bridges, president and founder of the Building Bridges Coalition, who led the protest march in Senatobia back in June. [Marquelle Bridges:] Thank you for having me. How are you both doing? We’re doing as well as can be. Really horrible stuff we’re going to be talking about here. We appreciate your time. I want to start with the fact that the state called this police murder of a 1-year-old justified. The mother wasn’t interviewed, and the public hasn’t seen the video. Coen’s grandmother said the word “justified” has haunted her since Monday. What was your reaction when the attorney general’s decision came down? What does it tell you about who the system in Mississippi and across the country was built to protect? [Marquelle Bridges:] First, I want to clear up something. Hunter Foster was never called for a call for Valecia Wiley or Latoya. He was there for a completely separate incident, a perp allegation. They were reviewing footage. He killed this baby simply because a Walmart worker said somebody’s running. Five police officers ran outside, and we know the result. He didn’t know anything. All he knew was it was two women and a baby. I want to clear that up. Valecia Wiley, Coen’s mother, is not accused of stealing anything. She hasn’t been charged with anything. We’ve been saying since day one, release the footage. They intentionally started the footage with them walking out the door to confuse people. If they started it in the store, you would see them at self-checkout paying for the diapers. It’s a lot of lies and false narratives started by the police. The initial statement was a lie. Tate County Sheriff’s Office said they were responding to a perp allegation. Senatobia Police tried to cover it up, saying they were responding to a shoplifting call. Walmart hasn’t pressed any charges. The police haven’t pressed any charges. They haven’t shown us any footage from inside Walmart. If they could show us these two Black women stealing, they would have done that day one. All of this is propaganda, just like the propaganda of her showing Hunter Foster that baby Coen was in the car in an attempt to get him not to shoot as her using the baby for a human shield. I just wanted to dispel some of these false narratives. I appreciate you doing that because every single news article has opened the story with the narrative that there was a call about shoplifting. Even if there was shoplifting, it does not justify a police officer pulling out a gun and shooting somebody. Every article has opened with the narrative that there was a call about shoplifting. That’s incredible what you’re saying because you often see the media jumping in to put the police’s narrative first. Thank you for clarifying that. Can you talk about your reaction to the idea that the Attorney General of Mississippi has labeled a police killing of a 1-year-old as justified? [Marquelle Bridges:] The label of 20 unarmed killings of Black people by police in 2023 and 2024 as justified is telling. Lynn Fitch overturned the conviction for the officer who killed George Robinson. Dexter Wade’s mother lost her son and her brother, and she overturned Anthony Fox’s conviction and paid him $75. Lynn Fitch lives in a plantation bought from the Ku Klux Klan. There hasn’t been any justice in Mississippi. There hasn’t been a Democratic elected person since 1861 in reconstruction. Our governor, Tate Reeves, was seen with Confederate flags and at Nazi parties, and he’s pictured in blackface. These people are the Klan, and it’s been happening. Nothing’s new. Emmett Till’s killer ended up being Governor Phil Bryant. Carolyn Bryant’s grandson ended up being the governor of the state. Emmett Till never received justice. It’s a long history. It’s expected. The only difference with this situation is with Nolan and baby Coen, we’re just saying we’re not taking it anymore. We don’t expect anything from this corrupt injustice system. It’s doing exactly what it was designed to do, which is disproportionately incarcerate people for slave labor. The 13th Amendment says no one can be treated like a slave unless incarcerated by the state. It’s no coincidence that Black people make up the majority of the prison system where you can still be treated like a slave. All of this is by design. We’ve seen this with Karmello Cyrus Belton in South Carolina denied justice. We’ve seen it with Carmelo Anthony. You can’t even defend yourself. We’ve seen it with Breonna Taylor. You can’t even sleep in your bed. Ahmaud Arbery. You can’t even go jogging. This is not the first 10-year-old Jordan Hill. A racist ran over a 10-year-old on an ATV. He was drunk, high, and left the scene. An all-white jury in Mississippi found him not guilty for killing the 10-year-old boy. This has been going on. I’m grateful to God now, because of hard work and a lot of these families retaining Ben Crump and the national attention he brings. Now people know about things we’ve been begging for help and crying out for change. Thank you for covering this and shedding light on what’s really going on. This past summer, the spate of racist killings, whether by police or in suspicious circumstances, has really grabbed national attention. We want to talk about the Nolan Wells case and this ruling of drowning. The grand jury says nothing to see here, this was a drowning, case closed. There’s a lot of evidence that points to the contrary. Can you talk about this demand for an investigation? What would justice look like in this case? [Marquelle Bridges:] That’s a better question for his parents and his family, but nobody has ever drowned with no water in their lungs and no water in their stomach. Bruising to the back of the head, bruising over his body, keeping his cell phone, all kinds of strange behavior. None of those boys were his friends or acted like friends. I’m not going to speculate, but it’s pretty clear what happened. They know what happened. Will this be another Emmett Till? We’re still asking what happened to Nolan Wells and Rasheem Carter in Mississippi. Rasheem was found decapitated in the KKK killing field with his parts in his mouth, and they said it was animals the same day he was found. This is Mississippi. If you get caught in a situation where you’re the only Black person, where the opportunity presents itself for you to be harmed, that’s what they’re going to do in these sundown towns. Mississippi has the largest and active Klan. It never stopped for us. The rest of the world moved forward. Nothing ever changed in Mississippi. I think it’s important to highlight this because a lot of people in other parts of the country might be familiar with the history of some of the things you’re talking about, but they see it as history. People who aren’t living in places like Mississippi might not understand that there are people in charge like the ones you’re talking about. The system, as bad as it is across the country, is significantly worse in places where Jim Crow mentality and Confederate mentality are in charge. Can you talk about the movement against this? We’ve seen protests from students at high schools to HBCU campuses demanding justice in both of these cases. Why is this hitting a younger generation so hard, and what does the organizing look like on the ground? [Marquelle Bridges:] This is the generation of warriors. This is the generation that’s going to fight back. They’re not easily fooled, bought, and sold, and they’re not believing anyone’s lies. They have information at their fingertips from a very young age. They can clearly see the truth. They know that what’s been happening and what’s happening now is not working, and they’re demanding a change as they should be. On the ground, we’ve moved to the by any means necessary approach. I wanted to offer something while we were on the subject of Attorney General Lynn Fitch and why this is happening. Rasheem Carter happened in 2022. That wasn’t a long time ago. In Mississippi, our Attorney General is in charge of prosecuting all officer-involved shootings. That started in 2022. Tell me why she would seek to dismiss Jaylen Lewis’s case, who was shot in the head by Capitol Police, and the only reason it didn’t get thrown out is because the judge stopped her. This is all political. She’s running for governor. All of this is being done on purpose. Before we let you go, can you talk about what’s next for the movement? Both families are calling for justice. There are still students organizing. What’s next? Is this going to be something you’re pressing for, like a federal investigation in the courts, or is this going to continue in the streets? [Marquelle Bridges:] What’s next? October 31st, there’s a vigil from 8:00 to 10:00 in Senatobia at City Hall for baby Coen. The next day, the organization SCAT is having a backpack giveaway and a celebration of life for his birthday in honor of baby Coen. That evening is going to be a block party celebrating his birthday. November 1st is the national mass protest for Nolan Wells. Ground Zero is going to have a mass march and rally. November 1st, Gulf Coast, Mississippi. November 2nd, we’ll be in Jackson, Mississippi at the Attorney General’s office. To answer the latter part of your question, we don’t have any faith in this current administration. Day one, the orange man signed an executive order to stop the DOJ from investigating all civil rights violations. We stalled a lot of families waiting on justice, not just in Mississippi. We don’t have any faith in this administration. They’re not seeking to help. They’re prosecuting little kids who make jokes online about Trump. They’re not prosecuting any real crime like the Epstein files. They’re not prosecuting any real injustice like what’s going on in the Black and brown community and with women. They don’t care about women’s health. They don’t care about babies or anyone. They only care about profit. We don’t have any faith. We have to wait on the next administration and hopefully get something done because there is no statute of limitations on murder. Those are our only avenues: either put pressure on the Attorney General to send it to a grand jury or bring in a special prosecutor and allow the grand jury to decide whether it’s justified or not, and then seek federal intervention. But with Trump, I just don’t see that happening. God is in control. We want to thank you for joining us to break all this down. We appreciate your analysis and all the work you’re doing. Hopefully, we can bring you back on again to continue to follow these developments. Thank you so much. [Marquelle Bridges:] Thank you so much, Justice for the Family Coalition.

articles.title: The Brazilian victory: left unity and digital autonomy
articles.author: Rezgar Akrawi
articles.content: The leftist leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic victory in Brazil’s presidential election on October 25, 2026. The result came amid intense political and social polarization and the growing influence of the far right in Brazil and across Latin America, backed by the US far right led by Donald Trump. The significance of this electoral victory extends beyond Lula securing a fourth term. It also lies in the political and organizational experience that helped make it possible, above all the ability of diverse left-wing and progressive forces, with different programs and ideological outlooks, to forge a broad electoral alliance around common ground in confronting the far right. A broad left-wing and progressive alliance despite differences Lula contested the election with the support of the “Brazil Ready for More” alliance, comprising seven left-wing and progressive parties organized into two party federations and two separate parties. The “Brazil of Hope” federation brought together Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Communist Party of Brazil, and the Green Party. The second federation united the Socialism and Liberty Party, which includes socialist and radical-left currents, with the Sustainability Network. The Brazilian Socialist Party and the Democratic Labor Party also joined the alliance, alongside supportive social movements and trade unions. Lula ran with Geraldo Alckmin of the Brazilian Socialist Party as his vice-presidential candidate. The importance of this alliance lies in its ability to bring together communists, socialists, the radical left, social democrats, and Greens despite their disagreements over capitalism, the role of the state, and the limits of social reform. These forces agreed on common electoral objectives while preserving their identities and organizational autonomy. This is one of the most important lessons of the Brazilian experience. Left unity does not require ideological or organizational uniformity. It means being able to work together on common ground while respecting pluralism and differences. Disagreements over Lula’s economic and social policies will naturally persist, including among the forces that supported him at the ballot box. Unity does not mean abandoning criticism or autonomy The Brazilian experience raises an important question for left-wing forces around the world. Why do ideological and organizational differences become barriers to cooperation, despite so much common ground, even when these forces face shared political and class challenges? Pluralism among communists, social democrats, the radical left, environmentalist and feminist currents, and independent leftists can be a source of strength and intellectual and political richness, provided it is managed democratically and constructively, without monopolization, exclusion, or claims to possess the absolute truth. Unity does not require abandoning criticism or offering unconditional acceptance of the policies of governments led by left-wing and progressive alliances. Confronting Capitalism and the far right requires a broad social front The victory demonstrated the importance of connecting the defense of democracy, rights, and freedoms with the economic and social demands of working classes and poor and marginalized communities. Lula drew broad support from lower-income groups and proposed expanding social assistance, improving living conditions, and defending democratic institutions. Confronting capitalism and the far right therefore cannot be confined to elections and party alliances. It requires sustained mass organizations in workplaces, neighborhoods, universities, trade unions, and social movements, together with policies that tackle class inequality and improve the lives of the majority. Digital autonomy: the fifth pillar of the left’s independence The Brazilian election revealed the growing importance of the digital sphere in political struggle. Social media platforms, algorithms, and artificial intelligence have become powerful tools in the hands of capitalist interests for shaping public consciousness and steering political debate. During the campaign, Lula’s supporters submitted complaints and evidence supporting allegations that Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and other platforms, showed digital bias in favor of his opponent. The company acknowledged “technical problems.” The dispute reached Brazil’s electoral court, which issued a ruling requiring Meta to apply equal standards to the candidates. The problem is not confined to Brazil. During Colombia’s most recent presidential election in 2026, journalistic investigations uncovered coordinated accounts and AI-generated fake videos targeting the left-wing camp , as well as shortcomings and bias in the platforms’ oversight of political advertising and content. In Germany, Elon Musk, the owner of X, publicly endorsed the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) during the 2025 election. He used his platform to promote the party’s positions and host its leaders, while several studies found a clear bias in the reach of the party’s content on the platform . Proving deliberate algorithmic bias is difficult because proprietary algorithms give capitalist corporations exclusive control over information about how they work and how content is ranked, amplified, or restricted. Without transparency, independent public and legal oversight, and access to the data needed for investigation, it is difficult to determine whether bias arises from algorithm design or deliberate intervention. Companies can easily attribute such problems to a “technical glitch”! The Brazilian experience also highlighted the importance of combining three interconnected arenas of struggle: mass struggle on the ground, legal action to hold digital platforms accountable and regulate their operations, and organized digital activism. Mass mobilization in the streets was accompanied by legal challenges against Meta and the development of a wide-ranging digital campaign that used social media effectively to reach millions of voters. This experience shows that the digital left’s struggle cannot replace grassroots struggle. It can reinforce and complement it. This is where digital autonomy emerges as the fifth pillar of the left’s independence, alongside ideological, organizational, financial, and media autonomy. Genuine political independence is no longer possible without a meaningful degree of autonomy over digital tools, platforms, and infrastructure, the protection of data, and the capacity for mass communication and organization free from the monopolistic control of capitalist corporations and major powers. Digital autonomy does not mean withdrawing from digital platforms. It means using them today with a critical, progressive awareness while working to develop open-source, democratically-governed digital alternatives and to build and strengthen independent technical capacities within the left. A left that fails to develop its digital autonomy and technological tools will remain at the mercy of its class adversaries in one of the most important arenas of contemporary political and social struggle. Lessons for the left worldwide The Brazilian experience cannot be reproduced mechanically. Every society has its own conditions and balance of class and political forces. The Brazilian approach to building alliances and working together can nevertheless offer valuable lessons. The unity the left needs is neither a single party nor a centralized leadership imposing its vision on everyone. It is flexible, democratic cooperation among diverse forces, grounded in common programs, respect for autonomy and pluralism, and meaningful participation by the grassroots, young people, and women. Such cooperation can be developed locally, regionally, and globally through different left-wing fronts and alliances on the ground, as well as digital left networks and internationals that contribute to the exchange of experience, coordinate shared initiatives and struggles, and work toward progressive digital alternatives. Lula’s victory offers an experience worth studying and learning from. It demonstrates the possibility of cooperation among left-wing forces despite their differences, while recognizing the other factors that contributed to the result. The left does not need to erase its diversity to unite. It needs to turn that diversity into an organized and effective force, strengthen its independence across all five pillars, and pursue the struggle for freedom, equality, and social justice while developing democratic, humanist socialist alternatives to capitalism. Rezgar Akrawi is a leftist writer and researcher focused on technology, AI, the digital revolution, and the development of contemporary leftist thought and practice in response to these transformations. He works as an expert in systems development and e-governance and is a theorist of the concept of the “Digital Left .” This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Western Sahara at a tipping point as US pushes for Moroccan ‘autonomy’ plan
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Large numbers of Sahrawi citizens took to the streets in El Aaiún , the largest city in Western Sahara, on Monday, to demand a just United Nations-sponsored solution that guarantees their right to freedom, self-determination, and independence. The demonstrations come as the United States allegedly pushes a draft UN Security Council resolution that would make Morocco’s autonomy plan the sole basis for negotiations over the future of the territory. The US-drafted text, reportedly circulated among Security Council members on October 22, has drawn strong objections from the Polisario Front, the Sahrawi independence movement, as well as human rights and solidarity organizations. Arguing the proposal risks predetermining the outcome of negotiations by placing Morocco’s plan over Western Sahara at the center of the process, rather than allowing the Sahrawi people to freely decide their political future. The dispute comes as the Security Council considers the future of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), established in 1991 to support the UN-OAU Settlement Plan, which included a referendum on self-determination. Polisario Front warns it could withdraw from the peace process In a letter from October 22 to Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the United Nations and current president of the Security Council, Dr Sidi Mohamed Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative to the UN, strongly rejected the US zero-draft. Omar said the text “fully reflects the national position of the penholder as well as that of Morocco, the occupying state,” describing it as “another extremely dangerous, unprecedented departure” from international law and the UN framework governing Western Sahara’s decolonization. He added that the process cannot be reduced to Security Council Resolution 2797 (2025), but must be understood within the wider body of relevant UN resolutions and the original agreement underpinning MINURSO. The mission was established under Resolution 690 (1991), following an agreement between the Polisario Front and Morocco, based on the UN-OAU Settlement Plan. According to the Polisario Front, changing the framework unilaterally would align the mission with Morocco’s position and undermine international efforts to resolve the territory’s status through decolonization. “The non-compliance of Morocco, the occupying state, with its commitments under the UN-OAU Settlement Plan, which was adopted unanimously by the Security Council, cannot justify any infringement upon the inalienable right of the Sahrawi people to self-determination and sovereignty over their homeland,” Omar wrote. Emphasizing that the text “cannot constitute a basis for any deliberations on MINURSO or the peace process in Western Sahara” and warned that, if it passed without “substantive and meaningful changes,” the movement “would have no choice but to disengage from the peace process as a whole.” But remains committed to a just, lasting, and definitive peace. Morocco’s autonomy plan One of the main concerns raised by the Western Sahara Research Watch (WSRW) is the reported change in the language of the draft. The text reportedly describes Morocco’s autonomy proposal as the “only basis” for negotiations, strengthening the language of the 2025 resolution, which referred to it as “a basis.” The WSRW argues that the difference is substantial. While autonomy could theoretically be one option freely chosen by the Sahrawi people, making Morocco’s proposal the sole basis in advance risks narrowing the political choices available to them. The organization asks, “How can the people freely determine the territory’s future if negotiations may only take place within a model that presupposes Moroccan sovereignty?” Going farther, the draft describes autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the most feasible solution. This shifts the purpose of negotiations away from determining Western Sahara’s status and towards negotiating the terms of Moroccan control. The WSRW also warns that the draft’s references to consulting Sahrawis in the territory, in refugee camps, and throughout the diaspora do not guarantee that they will have a decisive role in determining the outcome. “Being heard is not the same as being allowed to decide,” the organization argues. The European Association of Lawyers for Democracy and World Human Rights (ELDH ) has also called on the United Nations to uphold international law and the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination. International law and the question of sovereignty The Campaign for the Right to Self-Determination of the People of Western Sahara (CODESA) has also rejected the premise that international recognition of Morocco’s claim can determine the territory’s legal status. “Recognition by third states cannot turn occupation into sovereignty,” the organization argues. Western Sahara remains on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories. In its 1975 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that the materials and information presented to it did not establish any tie of territorial sovereignty between Western Sahara and Morocco that would displace the application of self-determination through the free and genuine expression of the territory’s people. CODESA also points to the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/37, adopted in 1979, which deplored Morocco’s continued occupation of Western Sahara and reaffirmed the right of the Sahrawi people to self-determination and independence. It further cites the UN Legal Counsel’s 2002 opinion on the legality of resource exploration in the territory and the 2024 rulings of the Court of Justice of the European Union, reaffirming Western Sahara’s separate and distinct status from Morocco. CODESA maintains that a political outcome cannot be declared in advance and then presented as self-determination. It invokes UN General Assembly Resolution 1541 (XV), which sets out principles relevant to the exercise of self-determination, including that integration with another state must result from the freely expressed wishes of the people through an informed and democratic process. The organization also objects to the United States’ prominent role as facilitator, arguing that a mediator that has already recognized Morocco’s claim cannot be assumed to be impartial. It maintains that negotiations must allow the parties to present their positions without imposing one party’s proposal as the only acceptable framework. “Negotiations in which only the occupying power’s proposal may be discussed are not negotiations; they are terms of surrender offered to the occupied people,” CODESA says. Over the years, Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara has gained diplomatic support as several countries have shifted their positions towards recognizing Moroccan sovereignty over the disputed territory rewarded by trade deals. But these diplomatic changes have not resolved the central question of Western Sahara’s future, and the right of the Sahrawi people to determine their own political status.

articles.title: Dockworkers at 110 ports worldwide strike against war and genocide
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Dockworkers across five continents and more than 110 ports launched a second historic international day of action against militarization and genocide on October 30. “We no longer want to work for war nor to pay for it,” José Nivoi of the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers (Coordinamento Autonomo Lavoratori Portuali, CALP) in Genoa said as actions kicked off. “Because the conditions we’re experiencing in Italy today, they’re the same conditions being experienced on five different continents.” Ports must serve life, not destruction The port workers’ actions are grounded in the Istanbul Declaration adopted earlier this year, which analyzes the impact of the growing arms transports on work in harbors worldwide. In the declaration and the interventions that followed, dockworkers outlined how this trend comes hand in hand with the erosion of working conditions, including the contractualization of work and aggressive austerity cuts. Friday’s actions are supported by roughly 25 unions from Australia to the United States and Uruguay, and from India to Mexico. A notable cluster of ports is located across the Mediterranean, where the first day of action – held in February this year – was launched. The dockworkers’ union ENEDEP led the strike call in Greece, receiving support from education workers and school children. Source: PAME International/Flickr Over the past months, dockworkers from Italy, the Basque Country, Turkey, Greece , and Morocco were joined by others. The expanded list added organizations from Croatia, Cyprus, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland , Montenegro, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden. “Our message is clear: dockworkers don’t work for war,” the Moroccan Democratic Labor Organization (Organisation Démocratique du Travail, ODT) from Tangiers port said at a press conference in late October. “Ports must serve life, transporting food and medicines that sustain our communities. They must be places of cooperation between peoples, never instruments of destruction.” No harbor for genocide A notable emphasis throughout the day is dockworkers’ solidarity with Palestine, including expressions of support from the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and the Global Sumud Flotilla . “With over 90% of Israeli imports arriving by sea, ports around the world are the chokepoint of Israel’s apartheid economy,” BDS and other organizations wrote on social media. “On October 30, dockworkers will show that, together, we can break the chain supplying Israel’s genocide, apartheid and occupation.” While the role of Mediterranean ports in fueling the genocide in Gaza has been more publicly exposed, the role of harbors in other regions remains perhaps less visible. That is precisely why the participation of dockworkers from Asia in the second international day of action is so significant. Read more: Indian port workers refuse to handle military cargo bound for Israel “In the last year, India’s major ports have been conduits from Indian public and private sector companies exporting to Israel’s Elbit Systems factories in Yokneam and Ramat Hasharon,” BDS and others wrote . “These factories manufacture artillery, munitions and ammunitions that has been documented to have been used in the genocide in Gaza.” “We firmly believe that support for Palestine should be channeled through our states, because today Israel enjoys a level of international impunity that allows it to carry out a genocide,” Nivoi said on Friday. “Therefore, we emphasize today that people must mobilize – not only in response to the rising cost of living, but above all to definitively liberate Palestine from Zionism.” Dockworkers’ action converges into general strike in Italy Italy and Genoa in particular have been a key node for building trade union solidarity with Palestine since 2023. Conscious of the links between growing militarization, imperialist drives around the world, and hardening austerity in Italy, CALP and the grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) also called for a convergence of local movements – leading to a new general strike . According to early estimates , approximately 2 million people in Italy responded to this call, including many students and young people. Over the past weeks, as students in several European countries took to the streets, youth groups across Italy have also been demonstrating against cuts to essential services. Read more: Italian government to deploy troops to Milan after anti-austerity protests On Friday, these groups promptly responded to the general strike call. “The student-worker alliance is growing ever stronger: across the country, students and young people are mobilizing – through occupations, encampments, assemblies, and demonstrations – against the government, while also promoting the upcoming general strike,” Marta Collot from the left party Potere al Popolo emphasized ahead of the day of action. “Labor can stop war” While witnessing the continuity of dockworkers’ actions in one part of the world brings much inspiration, trade unionists involved in preparing the day also emphasized the significance of the initiative expanding. Not all organizations were in a position to launch a strike, but they still recognized the importance of sending an anti-militarist message from their docks. In a comment for BreakThrough News , trade unionists from the Port of Vukovar, Croatia – mapped alongside unions taking part in the day of action – stressed the importance of dockworkers’ anti-war campaigning. Their point was concrete: wars fought elsewhere reshape livelihoods, shipping routes, and working conditions at home. Dockworkers in Koper, Slovenia, were among those joining the dockworkers’ second international day of action. Source: SŽPD/Facebook Yet the struggle is not only for dockworkers to fight, European trade unionists insist. As USB’s Francesco Staccioli pointed out in late October, the struggle against war remains a wider struggle for workers’ rights and social justice. Because of this, he emphasized, October 30 should be taken as a starting point to widen the scope of action further. “Labor can stop war. It can stop the genocide of the Palestinian people. It can stop imperialist aggression,” he said.

articles.title: One year after the election killings, Tanzania still awaits justice
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: One year ago, Tanzanians went to the polls in an election followed by deadly protests and a violent security crackdown. The immediate unrest has since subsided, but the wounds remain, and the demand for justice continues. President Samia Suluhu Hassan was declared the winner with 97.66% of the vote, an overwhelming margin that came with the exclusion of opposition forces and mounting restrictions on political activities. The disputed election and the violence that followed exposed deep tensions over Tanzania’s political realities, democratic participation, and the state’s response to dissent. A year on, not a single official has been held responsible, and justice for the victims and their families remains out of reach. A disputed election and a deadly crackdown The violence of October 2025 did not erupt out of nowhere. In the months before the election , opposition parties faced mounting restrictions, rallies were disrupted, and political activists were arrested. Opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason, which kept him out of the electoral process. His party, CHADEMA, was then excluded from the election after refusing to sign the electoral code of ethics. These developments narrowed the space for political competition and raised serious questions about the credibility of the vote. When Tanzanians went to the polls on October 29, demonstrations broke out in several parts of the country, including Dar es Salaam, Arusha, and Mwanza. Protesters rejected the election and demanded political change. The government responded with a nationwide curfew and an internet shutdown that lasted several days, cutting off communication and the flow of information as security forces confronted demonstrators. Human rights organizations documented the use of lethal force against protesters and other people who did not pose an imminent threat to life. The scale of the killings became clearer in April 2026, when a government-appointed Commission of Inquiry reported that at least 518 people had died during the election-related violence. Thousands were also injured. The opposition has maintained that the death toll was higher, with concerns also raised about people who remain missing and the circumstances in which bodies were removed from hospitals and mortuaries. The commission submitted its report to President Samia Suluhu Hassan on April 23. However, the full report has not been made public, leaving victims’ families and the wider public without access to the complete findings. One year later, impunity remains On October 28, Amnesty International marked the anniversary by condemning the continuing failure to hold officials accountable for the violence. “Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa. The organization also warned that, instead of opening a transparent accountability process, the authorities had increasingly used counterterrorism laws against opposition supporters and government critics. The withholding of the inquiry report has become a central obstacle to establishing the truth. Without public access to the findings, it remains difficult to scrutinize the evidence, understand the circumstances surrounding individual deaths, and determine what action the government intends to take against those responsible. President Samia Suluhu Hassan and other government officials have repeatedly portrayed the protests as a foreign-backed attempt to overthrow the government, a coordinated plot to destabilize the country. Activists argue that this narrative serves to deflect responsibility, evade justice, and excuse the authorities’ slow response to the killings. Tanzania today is marked by silence, not reconciliation. And a nation cannot simply move on from an atrocity of this scale without truth and accountability.
